options.content: Compression after which the original file can be rebuilt exactly
options.rationale: Correct: no data is lost.

options.content: Compression that removes data people are unlikely to notice
options.rationale: That describes lossy compression.

options.content: Compression that keeps the file the same size
options.rationale: Lossless compression does make files smaller.

options.content: Compression that only works on sound files
options.rationale: Lossless methods work on any kind of file.

explanation: Lossless compression stores patterns more efficiently; decompression gives back every original bit.

stem: Which of these is a reason for compressing a file?

options.content: It can be sent in less time over a network
options.rationale: Correct: a smaller file uses less bandwidth and transfers faster.

options.content: It improves the quality of the image
options.rationale: Compression never improves quality; lossy compression reduces it.

options.content: It makes the file impossible for hackers to read
options.rationale: That is encryption, not compression.

options.content: It adds a check digit to detect errors
options.rationale: Error detection is a different topic.

explanation: Reasons: less storage, less bandwidth, faster upload/download, smoother streaming, meeting file size limits.

stem: Which method is an example of **lossy** compression for an image?

options.content: Run-length encoding
options.rationale: RLE is lossless.

options.content: Storing repeated patterns once
options.rationale: Storing patterns more efficiently is a lossless idea.

options.content: Encrypting the pixel values
options.rationale: Encryption hides data; it is not compression.

options.content: Reducing the colour depth
options.rationale: Correct: colour data is permanently removed.

explanation: Lossy image methods: reduce colour depth or resolution, merge similar colours. RLE and pattern storage are lossless.

stem: Which file should be compressed with **lossless** compression?

options.content: A song streamed to listeners' phones
options.rationale: Music is usually compressed with lossy methods.

options.content: A photo on a news website
options.rationale: Web photos are usually compressed with lossy methods.

options.content: A spreadsheet of a school's exam marks
options.rationale: Correct: every number must be exactly right after decompression.

options.content: A video of a football match
options.rationale: Video is usually compressed with lossy methods.

explanation: Text, numbers and programs must be exact, so lossless compression is used.

stem: Why is lossy compression unsuitable for a program (executable) file?

options.content: Program files are too small to compress
options.rationale: Program files can be large; size is not the issue.

options.content: Changing even one bit could stop the program working
options.rationale: Correct: program instructions must be exactly the same after decompression.

options.content: Lossy compression only works on text
options.rationale: Lossy compression is used mainly on images, sound and video.

options.content: Programs are stored in hexadecimal, not binary
options.rationale: Programs are stored in binary like all data.

explanation: Lossy compression permanently removes data. Missing or changed instructions would make the program fail or behave wrongly.
hints: What would happen if some instruction bits were removed?

stem: For which data would run-length encoding give the **greatest** reduction in size?

options.content: A sentence of text with few repeated letters next to each other
options.rationale: Text rarely has long runs; RLE would barely help or make it bigger.

options.content: A photo with constantly changing colours
options.rationale: Changing colours give runs of length 1, which RLE stores badly.

options.content: A row of 40 white pixels followed by 20 black pixels
options.rationale: Correct: only two long runs, so just two pairs are stored.

options.content: A row of pixels that alternate black, white, black, white
options.rationale: Every run is length 1, so RLE doubles the size.

explanation: RLE works best with long runs of identical values; 60 pixels become 2 pairs.
hints: RLE replaces each run with a count and a value.

stem: Which method can be used for **lossy** compression of a sound file?

options.content: Run-length encoding the samples
options.rationale: RLE is lossless.

options.content: Increasing the sample rate
options.rationale: Increasing the sample rate makes the file larger.

options.content: Adding a parity bit to each sample
options.rationale: Parity bits are for error detection and add data.

options.content: Removing frequencies that people cannot hear
options.rationale: Correct: perceptual coding removes sounds people are unlikely to notice.

explanation: Lossy sound methods: reduce sample rate or resolution, remove sounds outside human hearing or masked by louder sounds.

stem: After lossy compression, the original file can be restored exactly by decompressing it.
explanation: False. Lossy compression permanently removes data; only lossless compression rebuilds the original exactly.

stem: Run-length encoding can make a file larger if the data contains very few repeated values next to each other.
explanation: True. Each run of length 1 becomes two values (count and value), so the data can double in size.

workedSolution:

explanation: RRR + WWWWW + RR + BBBB = RRRWWWWWRRBBBB (14 pixels). The original is rebuilt exactly, so RLE is lossless.

stem: Match each file with the most suitable type of compression.

left.content: A video clip shared in a chat app

explanation: Media that tolerates a small quality loss (music, photos, video) → lossy. Programs and data that must be exact (installer, spreadsheet) → lossless.

stem: Explain how run-length encoding compresses data.

points.description: It finds runs of identical consecutive values (e.g. pixels of the same colour).
Each run is replaced by one copy of the value and a count of how many times it repeats.
This stores fewer values when runs are long; no data is lost, so the original can be rebuilt (lossless).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: RLE looks for runs of the same value repeated one after another, such as 12 white pixels in a row. Each run is stored as a pair: the number of repeats and the value, e.g. 12W. When runs are long this needs far fewer values, and because the counts are exact the original can be rebuilt with no loss.

hints: What is stored instead of the run?

stem: A tour company in Victoria Falls puts high-quality photos of its trips on its website. Many customers view the site on phones using mobile data. Discuss whether the company should use lossy or lossless compression for the photos.

points.description: Lossy compression gives much smaller files, so pages load faster and use less mobile data.
Lossy permanently removes some detail / colours, so quality is slightly reduced.
Lossless keeps full quality, but files are larger, so pages load slowly on phones.
Justified conclusion, e.g. lossy, because the small loss of quality is hardly noticed on a phone screen and speed matters more to customers.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lossy compression would make the photos much smaller, so the website loads quickly on phones and uses less of customers' data, although some detail is lost permanently. Lossless compression would keep every detail, but the files would stay large and slow to load. Lossy is the better choice, because on a small phone screen the slight loss of quality is hardly noticed, while slow pages would put customers off.

explanation: Weigh file size and speed against quality, then conclude for this context.
hints: Give a point for and against each method.
Finish with a recommendation linked to the customers.

stem:
A school logo in Mutare uses only black (B) and white (W). One row of the logo is:

**BBBBBBBBWWWWWWWWWWWWBBBB**

Each colour code and each count is stored in 1 byte.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Write the row using run-length encoding, as count then colour (for example 3W).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bytes saved by the compression for this row.
parts.explanation: Original 24 bytes; RLE 3 × 2 = 6 bytes; saved 18 bytes.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Original 24 bytes; RLE 3 × 2 = 6 bytes; saved 18 bytes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which statement about the compressed logo is true?

options.content: Some pixels are lost permanently
options.rationale: That would be lossy compression.

options.content: It can be rebuilt exactly
options.rationale: Correct: RLE is lossless.

options.content: Its colours are reduced to grey
options.rationale: RLE keeps every colour value.

options.content: It has a lower resolution
options.rationale: The number of pixels is unchanged.

parts.explanation: RLE stores counts exactly, so decompression gives back the original row.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why RLE suits this logo but would not suit a photograph of a sunset.

points.description: The logo has long runs of the same colour, so few (count, value) pairs are needed.
A photograph has many gradual colour changes, so runs are very short (often length 1).
Short runs mean RLE stores two values for almost every pixel, so the file would hardly shrink or could get larger.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The logo has large areas of one colour, giving long runs that RLE stores as just a few pairs. A sunset photo has gradually changing colours, so almost every pixel differs from the next; RLE would store a count and a value for nearly every pixel, so the file could even grow.

stem: Chipo records a 3-minute song for an online competition. The website accepts files of at most 4 MiB, but her recording is 30 MiB.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which type of compression is most likely to reduce the file below 4 MiB?

options.content: Lossless
options.rationale: Lossless sound compression usually reduces size much less than needed here.

options.content: Run-length encoding
options.rationale: Sound samples rarely repeat in long runs.

options.content: Encryption
options.rationale: Encryption does not reduce file size.

options.content: Lossy
options.rationale: Correct: lossy compression gives much greater reductions for sound.

parts.explanation: Reducing 30 MiB to under 4 MiB needs lossy compression.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe two ways lossy compression could reduce the size of her recording.

points.description: Reduce the sample rate (fewer samples per second).
Reduce the sample resolution (fewer bits per sample).
Or: remove frequencies outside human hearing / sounds masked by louder sounds (perceptual coding). One mark for describing that data is permanently removed.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She could reduce the sample rate, so fewer samples are stored each second, or reduce the sample resolution so each sample uses fewer bits. Compression software can also remove sounds people cannot hear. These changes permanently remove data, making the file much smaller.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State one drawback of the compression for the competition, and why it may not matter.

points.description: Drawback: some quality is lost permanently / the song is slightly less faithful.
May not matter: most listeners will not notice the difference, especially through phone speakers or headphones.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The song loses some quality that cannot be restored, but the removed data is chosen so most listeners will not notice it.

explanation: Lossy compression (lower sample rate or resolution, perceptual coding) is needed; quality loss is small and permanent.
hints: How much smaller does the file need to be?
Think about the sound settings you met in the sound lesson.
